newsitem.title: ANGOLA: U.N. says it won't completely abandon Angola.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says it won't completely abandon Angola.

text.p: On the eve of a scheduled pullout of United Nations peacekeepers from Angola, a top official said the world body would not completely abandon the country it helped transform from war to peace.

"We are not leaving Angola right away. The whole withdrawal plan is based on what the situation on the ground is like. We will only send home those troops whose job is finished, when it is finished," U.N. special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, told Reuters.

The United Nations deployed 7,000 troops to Angola in 1995 to help implement a 1994 peace deal between the MPLA government and the rebel UNITA movement. They had fought a bitter 19-year civil war since independence from Portugal in 1975.
The international community, which has funded the force known as UNAVEM at a cost of $1 million a day, has become impatient with both parties for dragging their feet.
The withdrawal of the U.N. mission, which is made up of troops including from Brazil, India, Zambia, Zimbabwe and Romania, was originally scheduled for the end of February.
U.N. spokesman David Wimhurst said the first of the U.N. battalions were set to withdraw in March and the rest over a five-month period.
"The U.N.'s withdrawal from here is certain to have a lot of negative implications" on Angola's economy, said Alex Aboagye, chief economist for the U.N. Development Programme in Angola.
He said the withdrawal would mean job losses for hundreds of Angolans and lost business for weak service industries.
"It is not unusual for people here to be paying $2,500 for a two-bedroomed apartment. I will venture to say that that will change pretty soon after the U.N. leaves," Aboagye said.
He said the U.N. presence also had negative economic impact.

"We have basically created an artificial economy in Angola that is not good. All this UNAVEM money has poured in here but it has not come backed by goods, so without meaning to, we have contributed a lot to the inflationary cycle here," he said. The annual inflation rate reached 12,000 percent in June.

One of the main causes of delay in the completion of the peace timetable is the question of the future role of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi -- in or out of a government of unity with the ruling MPLA led by President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
Senior UNITA official Abel Chivukuvuku told Reuters the question was close to being resolved.
